activity.title: "The intellectual becomes a slob after he is kidnapped by the army." When I was called to 14-month mandatory military service last summer, I believed this quote. In my mind, a year filled with almost permanent sleep deprivation, hostile barrack talk, and nationalistic indoctrination was to follow. But after 14 months in the National Guard, I think Berger’s quote is flawed. Instead, I’m with my Lieutenant, George Petrou: “You can learn from anything, anytime, and from anyone.” In the army, I’ve had incredibly unique learning opportunities: - Combat Training (which I graduated with the highest recognition available to my 180-strong class) - Anti-Tank Weaponry Specialisation (where I got to fire rockets using an RPG!) - And serving as Staff Sergeant, the highest rank available to a conscript, in a guardpost overlooking Cyprus' de facto border and Green Line. The army was most definitely not an academic haven in the conventional sense. But just because the delivery of education was through sweat and calluses instead of books and lectures, did not make it any less a source of wisdom. From the simple discipline of making your bed every morning, to the difficult skill of keeping calm in high stake environments, I’m grateful for my experience in the National Guard. As I leave this chapter of life behind me, I'm excited to apply everything I've learnt this last year in my life beyond the army. Onwards and upwards! ...more

Over the past year, AI has changed how Maybern operates in incredible ways. Our engineers rarely write code by hand anymore – custom coding agents take on larger and more complex features by the day. Our product agent has developed deep domain expertise in how Maybern works. Reconciliation agents find root-cause discrepancies in minutes that used to take hours. I can accomplish more in a day than I could in weeks before. A year ago this all sounded crazy. Today it's just how we work: AI taking work off our desks, instead of us babysitting it for marginal gains. Living that way taught us where agents deliver outsized ROI: the tools, context, and environment you design for an agent matter as much as the model. Often more. Most private fund managers can't get there yet, because the context an agent needs is locked away in people's heads, PDFs, and Excel files: how the fees actually work, how you treat certain cashflows in your net returns, how the waterfall actually runs, how your firm interprets the ambiguous clause in the LPA. None of it has existed in a form an agent can run. Taking work off your desk starts with converting that domain knowledge into infrastructure. That's exactly what Maybern is. For five years we've been encoding how funds actually work – the math, the terms, the interpretations – into software that runs them. Today we opened all of it – waterfalls, fees, allocations, performance, reporting – to our customers' agents. Deterministic math. A full trail behind every number. Output you can check in seconds instead of re-deriving for hours. That's what makes it safe to hand work over. The Maybern MCP is live – available to Claude, ChatGPT, or agents you build. And there's a lot more coming soon. Full post: https://lnkd.in/gsWXeZsp

We’re sharing what we learned building automated QC for robot-mounted and ego-camera training data. A broad VLM “pass/reject” judge was difficult to calibrate. Whole-video inputs improved failure recall but produced too many false positives; sparse sampling preserved good clips but missed rare failures. The better approach was to decompose QC into failure-specific measurements. For robot video, we built focused VLM linters using temporally labeled contact sheets, explicit tail-frame sampling, and rule-specific prompts for sensor corruption, incomplete demonstrations, unrecoverable mistakes, and action overlap. For ego video, classical features won. Starting from 6,124 candidate signals, a LightGBM model using 120 features: motion, optical flow, brightness-calibrated blur, pose, hand trajectories, duration, and embedding distances reached 0.8003 out-of-time AUC across 1,777 held-out clips. DINOv2, OpenCLIP, VLM prompting, collector-history features, and stacked meta-models did not improve the final system. We’re publishing the successful approaches, failed experiments, category-level tradeoffs, and practical lessons for teams building robotics and physical AI data pipelines. The best QC model is not always the most general model. It is the one whose inputs match the failure mode. Have a read! https://lnkd.in/ejex9fkJ With the Scale AI robotics team: Don McCullough , Mouli Sivapurapu , Natasha Z. Dadabhoy , Agustin Sansone , Joe Fox Jr. , Jackson Lee, Pragna Mannam , Conrado Mader Blanco , Andy Mates , among others!
